questions.q: In the registry MDM style, what does the hub actually hold?
options: Nothing at all — registry style has no hub
A complete copy of every record from every source system
Only reference data code lists, never master data
An index of pointers and match keys, not full golden records
questions.explain: Registry style keeps the hub lightweight — it points to where the authoritative record lives in each source system rather than storing full golden records centrally.

questions.q: Which MDM architecture style requires bidirectional synchronization, because source systems keep creating and editing records locally?
options: Consolidation
There is no style that requires bidirectional sync
Coexistence
Registry
questions.explain: Coexistence treats the hub as authoritative while still letting source systems edit locally, so changes have to flow both out to and in from every source.

questions.q: What is the main tradeoff of batch/file-based integration, per this lesson?
options: It's always the fastest mechanism available, with zero latency
It requires no scheduling of any kind
It only works for reference data, never for master data
It's simple and auditable, but data can be hours or a full day stale
questions.explain: A scheduled export/import is easy to build and audit, but it means consumers are reading data as of the last run, not the current moment.

questions.q: What does event-driven (publish-subscribe) integration decouple, according to this lesson?
options: Batch jobs from ever needing a schedule
The customer master from the product master entirely
The hub from needing to know who its consumers are, since each subscriber reacts independently to a published change
The entire MDM program from any need for data quality rules
questions.explain: The hub publishes a change event once; it doesn't need to track or call out to each consumer individually — subscribers pick up the event on their own.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn that the 'wrong' integration pattern can still work, at first?
options: Because MDM tools automatically correct a mismatched pattern
Because small volumes and forgiving usage can mask a freshness mismatch until load or a real scenario exposes it
Because all three mechanisms are functionally identical under the hood
Because there is actually no such thing as a wrong pattern
questions.explain: A nightly batch feeding a system that needed real-time data can work fine on day one, then fail visibly once someone needs truly current information, like a support call about a recent order.
